summary:
Marswalk Planner is a web map of Jezero Crater that turns eleven datasets from six NASA missions into one decision: is this walk safe today, and what science can the crew do on the way?
The crew picks a base and science stops. The app finds the safest path over a 20 m elevation model, avoids steep slopes and crew-drawn no-go zones, and gives a clear go or no-go with walking time, daylight, dust risk and oxygen left in each suit. At every stop it reads NASA’s CRISM mineral maps and names the minerals there and why they matter in the search for ancient life. Each plan also reports its own impact: steep ground avoided, the cost of the safe detour and science stops per EVA hour.
We tested it against the real rover. Over 40 stretches of Perseverance’s drive (40.7 km), 80% of our planned route lies within 100 m of the path NASA’s drivers chose (median gap 44 m), with half as much steep ground (3.0% against 6.6%).
It gives a crew one screen instead of a dozen archives, and it works offline. The same engine can plan Artemis moonwalks, rover drives, field geology and mountain rescue.
details:
What it does. Marswalk Planner helps the first astronauts at Jezero Crater plan a walk on Mars. Before anyone opens the airlock, it answers one question: can the crew walk this route safely today, and what science can they do on the way? The crew picks a base and the places they want to visit. The app finds the safest path over a real 20 m NASA elevation model, avoiding ground steeper than the crew’s limit. It then gives a clear GO, GO WITH CAUTION or NO-GO, with a reason for every check: suit time, oxygen, the Apollo walkback rule (could the crew still get home on backup oxygen from every point of the walk?), daylight, temperature, dust-storm season and radio line of sight to base. At every stop it reads NASA’s CRISM mineral maps and says what is there (carbonate, clay, olivine and others) and why that matters in the search for ancient life. It suggests science targets close to the route, explains why the route bends where it does, and compares the safest, fastest and science-rich options. It also scores whether the trip suits a suited crew or a robotic rover better. The crew can draw no-go zones over sand or boulders and log field reports with how sure they are, and every route re-plans around them. One click gives a printable EVA briefing, another a 3D fly-through of the walk.

How it works. Everything runs in the browser, with no server. An A* search over 2.4 million terrain cells finds the route, usually in under half a second. Slope comes from the MRO CTX stereo elevation model built for Perseverance’s landing. Walking speed on slopes comes from Apollo 14 traverse data and energy use from a load-carriage model at Mars gravity: the same models used by SEXTANT, the traverse planner built by NASA and MIT. Mars local time, sunrise and sunset use the algorithm behind NASA’s Mars24 clock. Weather combines Perseverance MEDA reports with 14 years of Curiosity REMS data. In total the app uses eleven datasets from six NASA missions, all bundled so it works with no internet.

How we checked it. We tested the planner against the real rover. We cut Perseverance’s drive into 40 stretches of about 1 km and gave the planner only the start and end of each. 79% of the planned route lies within 100 m of the path NASA’s rover drivers actually chose, with half as much ground steeper than 15° (2.9% against the rover’s 6.6%). The elevation model matches Perseverance’s own positions at all 708 rover waypoints (mean difference 0.9 m), and the Mars clock reproduces the sol numbers in NASA’s weather feeds.

Benefits and intended impact. A crew or mission control gets one screen and one decision instead of a dozen archives in different formats. Every plan shows its measured impact: the steep ground avoided compared with walking in a straight line, what the safer detour costs, science stops per EVA hour and the oxygen left per suit. Because it needs no connection to Earth, it works where a Mars crew would use it, with a 20-minute signal delay. Students and the public can use it too: anyone can plan a walk to the rocks that may hold signs of ancient life and see what it would take. The engine needs only an elevation model, so the same logic applies to Artemis moonwalks at the lunar south pole, first-pass rover drive planning, field geology on Earth and mountain search and rescue.

Tools and languages. JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with no build step. Leaflet for the map, three.js for the 3D view and globe, Python (NumPy, tifffile, Pillow) to prepare the NASA data, and Node.js to run the validation against Perseverance. Hosted on Netlify, code on GitHub. Runs on any laptop or phone browser; no special hardware.

How it is creative. NASA’s Mars Trek shows layers of data; Marswalk Planner turns them into a decision: a route, a verdict and a briefing. It joins orbital terrain, minerals, rover records and weather into one plan, so safety and science are weighed together rather than separately. It also learns from the crew in the field, and it proves itself against the real rover instead of asking judges to trust it.

Factors we considered. Crew safety comes first, so oxygen, walkback, darkness and steep slopes are hard limits that force a NO-GO. Honesty about uncertainty: every number is tagged “NASA terrain”, “Model” or “Your input”, and a “How sure are we?” panel lists what was checked. We state the limits openly: the 20 m grid cannot see single rocks (the 25 cm HiRISE layer is there to check by eye), and the suit oxygen figures are planning placeholders. We used only real NASA data, with no simulated values. It had to work offline, be clear to non-experts (a mission overview and a one-minute guided tour), and work on a phone.
